chapter_summary:
The era of general-purpose CPU scaling is ending. The industry is moving toward heterogeneous computing, where specialized accelerators handle specific workloads more efficiently than CPUs. This chapter explores the trends shaping the future of parallel architectures.

**Heterogeneous computing:**

Modern systems combine different types of processors to optimize for different workloads:
- **CPU:** General-purpose, handles sequential and complex tasks.
- **GPU:** Massively parallel, handles graphics and machine learning.
- **NPU (Neural Processing Unit):** Specialized for neural network inference. Used in smartphones (Apple Neural Engine, Qualcomm Hexagon) and edge devices.
- **TPU (Tensor Processing Unit):** Google's AI accelerator, optimized for matrix operations in TensorFlow.
- **DSP (Digital Signal Processor):** Specialized for audio, video, and signal processing.
- **FPGA (Field-Programmable Gate Array):** Reconfigurable hardware for custom accelerators.
- **ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit):** Custom chips for specific applications (e.g., Bitcoin mining, video encoding).

**Domain-specific accelerators:**

1. **AI Accelerators:**
   - **TPU v4:** 275 TFLOPS per chip, designed for training large models.
   - **NVIDIA Tensor Cores:** Integrated into GPUs, perform mixed-precision matrix multiply-accumulate.
   - **Apple Neural Engine:** 16-core NPU in the M1/M2/M3, designed for on-device AI inference.
   - **Intel Habana Gaudi:** AI training processor with high-bandwidth memory.

2. **Video Accelerators:**
   - Hardware encoders/decoders (e.g., NVIDIA NVENC, Intel Quick Sync) for H.264, HEVC, AV1.

3. **Cryptography Accelerators:**
   - AES-NI on x86 processors for hardware-accelerated encryption.
   - SHA extensions for hashing.

4. **Networking Accelerators:**
   - SmartNICs (e.g., NVIDIA BlueField, Pensando) that offload network processing from the CPU.

**Chiplets:**

A chiplet is a small, modular chip that can be combined with other chiplets on a single package. Instead of building one large monolithic die, the processor is composed of multiple chiplets connected by an interposer or advanced packaging.

Advantages:
- **Yield:** Smaller chiplets have higher manufacturing yield than large monolithic dies.
- **Cost:** Chiplets can be manufactured at different process nodes (e.g., CPU chiplets at 5nm, I/O chiplets at 7nm).
- **Scalability:** More cores can be added by adding more chiplets, without redesigning the entire chip.
- **Flexibility:** Different products can be created by combining different chiplets.

Examples:
- **AMD Zen 2/3/4:** CPU chiplets (CCD) and I/O chiplets (IOD) on a single package.
- **Intel Meteor Lake:** Compute tile, graphics tile, SoC tile, and I/O tile.
- **Apple M1 Ultra:** Two M1 Max dies connected by UltraFusion interconnect.

**Trade-offs: General-purpose vs. specialized:**

| Aspect | General-Purpose (CPU) | Specialized (Accelerator) |
|--------|----------------------|---------------------------|
| Flexibility | High | Low |
| Performance/Watt | Low | High |
| Programmability | Easy | Hard |
| Cost | Lower per unit | Higher per unit |
| Time to market | Fast | Slow |
| Best for | Diverse workloads | Specific workloads |

The trend is toward **system-on-chip (SoC)** designs that integrate CPU, GPU, NPU, ISP, and other accelerators on a single die or package. This provides the best of both worlds: general-purpose programmability for most tasks and specialized efficiency for common workloads.

**Future trends:**
- **3D stacking:** Stacking chiplets vertically to increase bandwidth and reduce latency (e.g., AMD V-Cache).
- **Photonics:** Using optical interconnects for higher bandwidth and lower power.
- **Neuromorphic computing:** Processors that mimic biological neural networks (e.g., Intel Loihi).
- **Quantum computing:** Still in early stages, but may eventually complement classical computing.

screens.title: Parallel Architecture Trends and Accelerators
screens.subtitle: Why specialization and modular packaging are reshaping modern processors

narration.text: We are at a turning point in processor design. Scaling general-purpose CPUs alone no longer delivers the energy efficiency and throughput required by today’s workloads, so architects combine different processor types and modular packaging to get more performance per watt. In this lesson you will learn the practical trends that drive heterogeneous computing: why dedicated NPUs, TPUs, DSPs, FPGAs, and ASICs coexist with CPUs and GPUs, how chiplets replace monolithic dies to improve yield and flexibility, and what trade-offs designers must weigh when choosing specialization over generality. You’ll see concrete product examples — AMD’s chiplet-based Zen designs, Intel’s tile approach, and multi-die Apple UltraFusion — and a clear way to reason about performance per watt, programmability, and time-to-market. By the end you should be able to explain why a data center might buy both GPUs and TPUs, why a handset vendor integrates an NPU into an SoC, and when chiplets make better business sense than a single large die. Think about the last system you used: which parts are specialized, and why might the designer have chosen that mix?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Heterogeneous processors plus modular chiplet packaging deliver higher efficiency and faster product iteration by matching hardware to workload and manufacturing realities.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter — overview and assessment milestones

narration.text: In this chapter you will develop four practical competencies that let you reason about modern processor design. First, you will describe the major parallel architecture trends — heterogeneous computing, domain accelerators, and chiplets — and explain why they matter for performance per watt. Second, you will identify and compare accelerators such as NPUs, TPUs, DSPs, FPGAs, and ASICs, and give examples of where each is used, like the Apple Neural Engine in phones or TPU units in data centers. Third, you will explain what chiplets are and why chiplet-based packaging improves yield, lowers cost, and enables flexible product lines, citing AMD’s CCD/IOD approach and Apple’s UltraFusion. Fourth, you will analyze trade-offs between general-purpose CPUs and specialized accelerators across flexibility, performance per watt, programmability, cost, and time to market. Each objective includes a short mnemonic to help you remember and a verified competency milestone to check understanding. These skills prepare you for design trade-off questions and for evaluating SoC and server choices in systems engineering.

narration.text: Now that you know the target competencies, let’s make them actionable. For describing trends, practice by categorizing a modern system: identify its C P U, G P U, NPU, and any ASICs or FPGAs. For accelerators, learn to state where each is best used — NPUs for low-latency on-device inference, TPUs for large-scale matrix training, DSPs for streaming audio and video, and FPGAs for reconfigurable pipelines. To show you understand chiplets, sketch a package that separates compute chiplets from an input and output die and explain why different nodes are chosen. To analyze trade-offs, write a short justification for choosing a TPU over a G P U or vice versa for a given AI workload, citing performance per watt and programmability concerns. Each practice item ties to a verified competency milestone: a brief written answer, a diagram, or a benchmark comparison. These tactics turn conceptual knowledge into evidence you can present to engineers or product teams.

screens.title: Heterogeneous Computing Explained
screens.subtitle: Why systems mix CPUs, GPUs, NPUs, and other engines

narration.text: Heterogeneous computing is the practice of combining different processor types in a system so each workload runs on the most suitable engine. Define each role: the C P U remains the generalist that manages control flow, input and output, and irregular tasks; GPUs are highly parallel and excel at the dense arithmetic in graphics and many machine-learning workloads; NPUs and TPUs are domain-specific units optimized for neural network inference and training respectively; DSPs handle streaming signal transforms; FPGAs provide reconfigurable pipelines; and ASICs are fixed-function chips for a single purpose. The practical benefit is higher performance per watt for common operations: a TPU or NPU often completes tensor operations using far less energy than a C P U because it removes general-purpose circuits and optimizes memory paths. A concrete example is a smartphone that uses its Apple Neural Engine for on-device inference to reduce latency and preserve privacy while delegating general UI tasks to the C P U. A common misconception is that accelerators always replace CPUs — they do not. Instead, they complement CPUs: CPUs orchestrate tasks, handle exceptions, and run code that is not worth offloading. Takeaway: think of heterogeneous systems as teams where each member has clear strengths; the design question is which tasks to delegate and how to move data efficiently between members.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Heterogeneous computing pairs specialized processors with CPUs so each workload runs on hardware optimized for it.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.6 › Heterogeneous Computing
Core Concept

Heterogeneous Computing

Different processors for different workloads improve efficiency and latency.

CPU
Control, branching, system orchestration
GPU
Massively parallel arithmetic
NPU / TPU
Optimized tensor ops, inference/training
DSP / FPGA / ASIC
Signal processing, reconfigurable logic, fixed functions
Why it matters
  • Higher performance per watt when computation matches hardware strengths.
  • Lower latency for on-device inference and improved privacy without cloud round trips.
  • Better total system throughput by offloading dominant kernels to accelerators.
Example
A phone uses its NPU for face recognition and the CPU for UI navigation. The NPU reduces energy per inference and avoids waking a larger CPU pipeline for every camera frame.
Key Takeaway

Treat processors as a team; delegate repetitive heavy arithmetic to accelerators and keep control logic on the CPU.

screens.title: Domain-Specific Accelerators
screens.subtitle: How TPUs, NPUs, DSPs, FPGAs, and ASICs differ and where each excels

narration.text: Domain-specific accelerators are hardware units built to excel at a narrow set of tasks. TPUs and NPUs specialize in tensor operations; they remove or simplify logic that is unnecessary for matrix multiply and memory movement, achieving higher performance per watt. DSPs focus on real-time streaming transforms for audio and video, offering low-latency signal pipelines. FPGAs are reconfigurable: you can map custom data paths for evolving workloads but with higher engineering effort. ASICs lock in a function and can reach the best efficiency when the function is stable, but they have long design cycles and limited flexibility. Consider the concrete differences: a TPU is ideal for large-scale matrix workloads and often used for training or optimized inference, while an NPU like Apple’s Neural Engine targets low-power on-device inference. A common misconception is that FPGAs are always slower than ASICs; in early deployment or for specialized logic, FPGAs can offer competitive latency while developers iterate. The practical design question is workload stability: if the computation kernel is stable, an ASIC may be justified; if it evolves, an FPGA or programmable accelerator is safer. Ultimately, system architects mix these choices to balance efficiency, flexibility, and development time.

keyIdea.title: Accelerator trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Choose accelerators based on workload stability, latency needs, and power targets; there is no one-size-fits-all.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.6 › Domain-Specific Accelerators
Comparison

Accelerator Types

Compare function, example products, and typical uses.

TPU
Matrix ops, high throughput training and inference. Example: Google TPU v4 for large models.
NPU
On-device inference, low-power. Example: Apple Neural Engine.
DSP
Streaming transforms for audio/video. Often built into SoCs.
FPGA / ASIC
Reconfigurable vs fixed; FPGAs for iteration, ASICs for production efficiency.
Guiding points
  • Performance per watt often improves when removing general-purpose circuitry.
  • Programmability cost rises as specialization increases; toolchains vary widely.
  • Time to market matters: FPGAs shorten iteration; ASICs minimize unit cost at scale.
Concrete example
Data centers may deploy GPUs for mixed workloads and TPUs for large-scale model training because TPUs deliver higher throughput for tensor math while GPUs remain versatile for other tasks.
Key Takeaway

Match hardware to workload stability and development timelines to choose the right accelerator.

screens.title: What is a Chiplet?
screens.subtitle: Modular dies assembled into a single package — defining the idea and its benefits

narration.text: A chiplet is a small die designed to be combined with other chiplets in a single package, replacing the single large monolithic die. The main motivation is manufacturing economics and design flexibility: large dies suffer from lower yield because the chance of a defect increases with area; by splitting functionality into smaller chiplets you increase the probability that each piece is good, lowering cost per usable package. Chiplets also let designers mix process nodes — for example, placing C P U compute chiplets on an advanced 5nm node and an input and output chiplet on a more mature 7nm node — reducing cost without sacrificing performance. This approach enables scalability: vendors can add more compute chiplets to increase core counts without redesigning the whole monolith. Concrete examples include AMD’s Zen-based CCD and IOD separation, Intel’s tile-based Meteor Lake with separate compute and input and output tiles, and Apple’s M1 Ultra that stitches two M1 Max dies with UltraFusion. Misconceptions to avoid: chiplets are not magic — they introduce packaging complexity, interconnect latency, and potential power overhead. The design balance is between yield and communication costs. The takeaway is simple: chiplets trade reduced manufacturing risk and faster product variety for added packaging and design complexity.

keyIdea.title: Chiplet concept
keyIdea.text: Chiplets split a processor into smaller dies to improve yield, lower cost, and enable flexible SKUs, at the cost of packaging and interconnect complexity.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.6 › Chiplets
Definition

Chiplets and Modular Packaging

Small dies combined in a package to improve yield and flexibility.

Yield
Smaller dies have higher manufacturing yield than a single large die.
Node mixing
Different chiplets can be manufactured on different process nodes to balance cost and performance.
Scalability
Add compute chiplets to scale core counts without redesigning all functions.
Examples
  • AMD Zen CCD + IOD
  • Intel Meteor Lake tiles (compute, graphics, I/O)
  • Apple M1 Ultra using UltraFusion to join two dies
Trade-offs
  • Pro: Higher yield and lower average cost per good die.
  • Con: Inter-chiplet latency and packaging complexity increase design challenges.
  • Con: Interconnect power and area may offset some gains.
Key Takeaway

Chiplets trade manufacturing risk for interconnect complexity — they are a practical way to scale cores and mix process nodes.

screens.title: Chiplet Manufacturing and Packaging Steps
screens.subtitle: From die fabrication to package integration and the impacts on yield

narration.text: Understanding the chiplet flow clarifies why chiplets are attractive. First, designers partition the SoC into functional chiplets — compute, input and output, memory, and accelerators — choosing a process node for each chiplet based on speed and cost. Second, each chiplet is fabricated independently; because chiplets are smaller, more of the wafer yields good dies, improving economics. Third, tested good chiplets are assembled into a package using interposers, embedded bridges, or die-to-die interconnects such as EMIB or UltraFusion. Fourth, the package testing and thermal design ensure the assembled device meets performance and reliability targets. Finally, system integration places the package on the motherboard or module. A concrete scenario: an x86 vendor manufactures C P U core chiplets on an advanced node and an input and output chiplet on an older, cheaper node to save cost while keeping compute fast. Misconceptions include assuming inter-chiplet communication is as fast as on-die links; in practice, packaging interconnects add latency and power overhead. The takeaway is that chiplet-based manufacturing improves yield and flexibility but requires careful interconnect and thermal strategies to approach monolithic performance.

keyIdea.title: Manufacturing flow
keyIdea.text: Partition → Fabricate → Test → Package → Integrate — each step affects yield, cost, and interconnect performance.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.6 › Chiplet Process Flow
Process Flow

From partition to integration

Five main stages show where yield and cost are affected.

1. Partition
Split SoC into chiplets and choose node per function.
2. Fabricate
Manufacture chiplets separately; higher yield per chiplet area.
3. Test
Identify good chiplets before packaging to avoid costly wasted packages.
4. Package
Assemble using interposers or die-to-die interconnects; watch latency and power.
5. Integrate
Place package in system and validate thermal and board-level behavior.
Concrete scenario
A vendor makes compute chiplets on 5nm for speed and an I/O die on 7nm to cut costs. Each good compute chiplet is tested and paired with a passing I/O die, improving effective yield against a single large 5nm die.
Key Takeaway

Manufacturing and packaging choices determine the economic advantage of chiplets; interconnect design determines performance overhead.

screens.title: General-Purpose vs Specialized Processors
screens.subtitle: A focused trade-off table so you can defend design choices

narration.text: Choosing between a general-purpose C P U and a specialized accelerator requires a structured trade-off. Consider five dimensions: flexibility, performance per watt, programmability, cost, and time to market. CPUs are flexible and easy to program, so they work for diverse workloads and rapidly changing requirements. Specialized accelerators, such as TPUs or ASICs, deliver much higher performance per watt because they remove unnecessary general-purpose logic and optimize memory and compute paths, but they are harder to program and have higher non-recurring engineering costs. Cost per unit can be lower for an ASIC at high volumes but higher for prototypes and low-volume runs. Time to market is often fastest with general-purpose hardware or with FPGAs for iteration, whereas developing an ASIC takes much longer. A concrete example: a cloud provider buying hardware for large-scale training may prefer TPUs for efficiency and throughput, while a mobile SoC vendor includes an NPU for on-device inference and a C P U for general tasks. A misconception is assuming specialized hardware is always cheaper — it is cheaper only when volumes and stable kernels amortize development costs. The practical skill is to balance workload predictability, expected volume, and acceptable engineering effort to choose the right mix.

keyIdea.title: Trade-off matrix
keyIdea.text: Balance flexibility, efficiency, programmability, cost, and time-to-market to pick CPU or accelerator.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.6 › General vs Specialized

General-Purpose vs Specialized

Use a five-dimension comparison to decide which suits your product.

Dimensions
  • Flexibility — CPU: high, Accelerator: low
  • Performance per watt — CPU: lower, Accelerator: higher
  • Programmability — CPU: easy, Accelerator: harder
  • Cost & Time to market — vary with volume
Concrete Example
For a high-volume training cluster, TPUs can provide better throughput per watt than general GPUs. For a phone, an integrated NPU improves battery life and latency for inference compared to sending data to the cloud.
Key Takeaway

Choose specialization when workload is stable and volume justifies the engineering cost; otherwise prefer general-purpose or reconfigurable options.

Misconception check
Specialized hardware is not inherently cheaper in low volume. Consider amortizing design costs, toolchain maturity, and expected kernel stability before committing.

screens.title: SoC Integration and Examples
screens.subtitle: How CPU, GPU, NPU, ISP and accelerators combine in modern SoCs

narration.text: System-on-chip integration is the practical answer to combining multiple engines while keeping power and latency low. An SoC typically integrates C P U cores, G P U blocks, NPUs or other accelerators, an image signal processor for camera pipelines, memory controllers, and input and output, all in a single package or die. The architecture groups components with high-bandwidth links so data movement for common tasks stays local and cheap. A concrete example is Apple’s family of SoCs, which include C P U clusters for general tasks, G P U clusters for graphics and parallel compute, an Apple Neural Engine for inference, and ISP blocks for camera processing — all tuned to their mobile power budget. Another example is an AMD Ryzen package using chiplets where compute chiplets provide cores and an input and output die handles memory and PCIe. A common misconception is that integrating more blocks always reduces power; in fact, integration reduces off-chip traffic but increases on-chip thermal density and design complexity. The key design choices are where to place accelerators relative to memory to minimize data movement and which functions benefit most from being fused on a single package versus left modular.

keyIdea.title: SoC architecture
keyIdea.text: Integrate complementary engines with high-bandwidth local links to minimize data movement and maximize efficiency for targeted workloads.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.6 › SoC Integration
Architecture

System-on-Chip Integration

Combine CPU, GPU, NPU, ISP and accelerators in one package to reduce latency and power per operation.

Local memory and interconnect
Place memory buffers close to accelerators to reduce data movement and energy.
Heterogeneous scheduling
Coordinating work across engines requires OS and runtime support to choose the best target.
Examples
  • Apple SoCs: CPU clusters, GPU, Neural Engine, ISP tuned for mobile use.
  • AMD packages: compute chiplets with I/O die for memory and I/O functions.
Design note
Integration reduces off-chip transfers but increases thermal density. Balance integration with cooling and interconnect design.
Key Takeaway

SoC design trades off integration benefits against thermal and design complexity; co-locate high-traffic elements to save power.

screens.title: Evolution: Monolithic Dies to Chiplets
screens.subtitle: A short timeline that captures the industry shift and motivations

narration.text: The move from monolithic dies to chiplet-based and tile-based designs happened as process scaling became more expensive and yields dropped for very large dies. Early generations emphasized monolithic integration: pack everything onto one large die to maximize on-die bandwidth. As die sizes grew, manufacturers faced exponentially lower yields. The chiplet approach emerged to solve this: break the design into smaller pieces, make them independently, and assemble them in a package. Vendors also pursued heterogeneous integration to put accelerators and controllers closer to memory and input and output. Concrete milestones include AMD’s Zen series splitting compute chiplets from an input and output die, Intel experimenting with tile-based designs such as Meteor Lake, and Apple using UltraFusion to bind multiple M1 variants into larger packages. Looking forward, 3D stacking and photonics aim to further reduce communication bottlenecks between elements. A misconception is viewing chiplets only as a yield hack — they are also strategic for product differentiation and mixing process nodes. The essential lesson is that packaging innovations can be as important as transistor scaling for system performance and cost. Evolution: Monolithic Dies to Chiplets means packaging and heterogeneity evolved because die scaling alone could not meet yield, cost, and energy targets.. In practical terms, a short timeline that captures the industry shift and motivations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Timeline takeaway
keyIdea.text: Packaging and heterogeneity evolved because die scaling alone could not meet yield, cost, and energy targets.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.6 › Evolution Timeline
Timeline

Monolithic → Chiplets → Heterogeneous Packaging

Key stages and motivations behind the industry shift.

Monolithic Dies
Everything on one die; high on-die bandwidth but lower yield as die area grows.
Chiplets & Tiles
Smaller dies assembled into packages to improve yield and enable node mixing.
Heterogeneous SoCs
Accelerators and specialized blocks integrated to reduce data movement and power for common tasks.
Examples
  • AMD: CCD + IOD chiplets
  • Intel: Meteor Lake tiles
  • Apple: M1 Ultra UltraFusion
Future directions
3D stacking, photonics and neuromorphic designs aim to further reduce communication costs and enable new workloads.
Key Takeaway

Packaging innovations often unlock more practical gains than raw transistor scaling; design trade-offs determine the best path forward.

screens.title: Interconnects and Communication Costs
screens.subtitle: Why inter-chiplet links and memory placement matter for performance

narration.text: Interconnect design is one of the central challenges for chiplet and heterogeneous systems. When components are on the same die, communication can use wide, low-latency buses and tightly coupled caches. With chiplets or tiles in a package, data crosses physical interconnects that add latency, consume power, and may reduce effective bandwidth. Designers mitigate these penalties by placing accelerators close to local scratchpads or by adding high-bandwidth memory channels. Packaging technologies such as 2.5D interposers, EMIB, and dedicated die-to-die bridges reduce latency compared to off-package links but still fall short of on-die wire speed. A concrete example: AMD’s chiplet systems use an internal fabric to move cache lines between CCDs and the input and output die; this fabric is fast but introduces measurable latency compared to a single monolithic cache hierarchy. A common misconception is treating interconnect cost as negligible; in many workloads, data movement dominates energy and runtime. The key design rule is to minimize data movement for hot data paths and to size local memories to keep frequently used tensors or buffers on-chip when possible. Interconnects and Communication Costs means design interconnects to minimize latency and energy for hot data paths; packaging can reduce but not eliminate communication costs.. In practical terms, why inter-chiplet links and memory placement matter for performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interconnect focus
keyIdea.text: Design interconnects to minimize latency and energy for hot data paths; packaging can reduce but not eliminate communication costs.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 10.6 › Interconnects & Communication
Architecture

Interconnects and Data Movement

Communication cost often dominates runtime and energy when components are modularized.

On-die vs Package vs Off-package
  • On-die: lowest latency, highest bandwidth.
  • Package (interposer/EMIB): higher latency than on-die, lower than off-package.
  • Off-package: highest latency and energy cost.
Mitigations
  • Local scratchpads for accelerators to reduce repeated transfers.
  • High-bandwidth memory channels and stacked dies for limited hot data.
  • Efficient coherence and cache strategies to reduce unnecessary traffic.
Concrete example
AMD uses an internal fabric to move cache lines between CCDs and the I/O die. This fabric is optimized for speed but still creates extra hops compared to a single monolithic cache plane.
Key Takeaway

Treat interconnect design as central: minimizing hot-path data movement often yields larger gains than raw compute improvements.

screens.title: Emerging Directions: 3D Stacking, Photonics, Neuromorphic
screens.subtitle: Where packaging and novel computation models may lead next

narration.text: Beyond chiplets, several forward-looking ideas aim to change how components communicate and compute. 3D stacking places dies vertically to shorten interconnects and increase bandwidth; examples include stacked caches or memory-on-top-of-logic. Photonics proposes optical interconnects for very high bandwidth and low power for certain links, potentially reducing electrical signaling bottlenecks in large systems. Neuromorphic computing mimics biological neurons and synapses to process specific classes of problems like spiking neural net models with different efficiency profiles. Quantum computing remains early-stage but may eventually provide complementary capabilities for particular problem classes. These technologies are not replacements for accelerators today; they are potential complements that change the cost-benefit calculus of integration. A misconception is assuming immediate practicality — many of these techniques are research-intensive and require co-design of hardware and software stacks. The takeaway is to monitor these trends as options that can reduce communication costs or unlock new algorithmic efficiencies, and to evaluate them against the maturity, software ecosystem, and target workloads of your product. Future Trends

3D Stacking, Photonics, Neuromorphic

Emerging approaches that change communication and computation trade-offs.

3D Stacking
Vertical dies reduce link length and increase bandwidth for memory-heavy workloads.
Photonics
Optical links can provide high bandwidth at lower power for certain interconnects across packages.
Neuromorphic
Architectures inspired by brains that may excel at sparse, event-driven workloads.
Practical note
Each approach has software and packaging challenges. Adoption depends on demonstrated system-level gains and ecosystem maturity.
Key Takeaway

Watch for technologies that reduce the cost of moving data; these can change the balance between specialization and integration.

screens.title: Design Exercise: Analyze a Real Product
screens.subtitle: How to evaluate a chiplet or heterogeneous SoC and defend the architecture

narration.text: Apply what you’ve learned by researching a recent processor or SoC that uses chiplets or heterogeneous integration, and create a short analysis. Start by listing the components you find: C P U chiplets, G P U, NPU, memory, and input and output. Sketch a simple block picture showing how these pieces connect and label which elements are on advanced nodes and which use older nodes. Then ask why the vendor chose this approach: yield, cost, scaling, or feature differentiation. For the accelerator, pick a benchmark or workload and reason about performance per watt versus a C P U-only design — for example, explain whether a TPU or G P U would be better for a particular model and why. Common mistakes are assuming every accelerator reduces cost or that mixing nodes always saves money; include interconnect and packaging overheads in your reasoning. Finally, prepare a two-paragraph justification that defends the overall architecture choice and presents one potential improvement, such as adding local scratchpad memory to an accelerator. This exercise converts conceptual knowledge into a defensible engineering argument you can present to teammates or include in a design review.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three essential concept cards from this chapter

narration.text: Let’s close with three compact ideas to carry forward. First, heterogeneous computing pairs CPUs with specialized accelerators — NPUs, TPUs, GPUs, DSPs, FPGAs, ASICs — to increase performance per watt for targeted workloads while keeping a C P U for control and irregular tasks. Second, chiplets let designers break large dies into smaller, independently manufactured pieces, improving yield and enabling node mixing; that approach trades off packaging complexity and inter-chiplet latency against cost and scalability. Third, the decision to use general-purpose or specialized hardware depends on workload stability, volume, and acceptable engineering effort: accelerators can be orders of magnitude more efficient for narrow problems but require investment in tooling and integration. Remember also that interconnects and memory placement often determine real system performance, so reduce hot-path data movement when possible. Keep these three core ideas in mind as you analyze SoC and server architectures: hardware is a set of trade-offs, and the right design depends on workload, cost, and schedule.

keyIdea.title: Three takeaways
keyIdea.text: Heterogeneity, chiplet economics, and trade-off-driven design choices are central to modern parallel architecture.

Module 11 › Chapter 10.6 › Key Concepts

Key Concepts

Three compact cards to remember the chapter’s essentials.

Heterogeneous Computing
Use CPUs, GPUs, and accelerators together to match hardware to workload demands for efficiency.
Chiplets & Packaging
Split large dies into smaller chiplets to improve yield, cost, and product flexibility.
Trade-offs
Weigh flexibility, performance per watt, programmability, cost, and time to market when choosing hardware.
Summary
Architectural choices hinge on workload characteristics and economics; specialized accelerators and modular packaging are tools to optimize those trade-offs.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Compact Cards
screens.subtitle: Three short concept cards you can recite quickly

narration.text: As a final quick-reference, memorize these three one-sentence cards. First, heterogeneous systems assign work to engines that are best suited for that work to improve energy and latency characteristics. Second, chiplets reduce manufacturing risk by splitting large dies into smaller pieces and enable node mixing, but they introduce packaging and interconnect overheads. Third, the general-purpose versus specialized decision requires balancing programmability and flexibility against performance per watt and unit cost; volume and workload stability decide which side wins. Use this compact set when you need to explain the chapter succinctly in a meeting or when defending an architectural choice. Ask yourself: which workloads dominate my system, and which costs — development, unit, or power — matter most? That question is the practical lens this chapter gives you.
